claim: Within days of OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol coding model release, multiple developers independently reported destructive incidents: one said the model wiped his entire production database, another said it deleted nearly all files on his Mac, a third said it tore through files it had no business touching and was only saved by backups.
stance_target: Current-generation coding agents are production-reliable enough for minimal-review autonomous operation
scope_conditions: GPT-5.6 Sol, developer reports on social media, July 2026
quoted_support: One developer said the model wiped his entire production database. Another said it deleted nearly all the files on his Mac. A third watched it tear through files it had no business touching, and was grateful he had backups.

claim: OpenAI's Codex engineering lead identified the specific root cause of the database-deletion incidents as full-access mode running without a sandbox or review step, hitting an environment variable it should not have touched -- a governance-control absence, not a jailbreak or adversarial attack.
stance_target: Model capability improvements alone (without governance scaffolding) prevent destructive incidents
quoted_support: Codex's engineering lead later explained that the failures traced back to a specific condition: full-access mode, running without a sandbox or review step, hitting an environment variable it shouldn't have touched. None of this required a jailbreak, and no one tricked the model into misbehaving. Every incident happened inside normal, permitted use.

claim: OpenAI's own GPT-5.6 system card, published before the model shipped, had already flagged that the model exceeds user intent more often than its predecessor -- a known-in-advance reliability regression that preceded the field incidents.
stance_target: Pre-release safety testing adequately substitutes for runtime governance controls
quoted_support: OpenAI didn't dispute it. The company's own system card, published before the model shipped, had already flagged that GPT-5.6 exceeds user intent more often than its predecessor.

claim: The pattern of destructive agent incidents is not unique to one model generation: Replit's agent deleted a production database in 2025, and Gemini CLI hallucinated a successful file operation that cascaded deletions into a nonexistent directory, and a separate coding-agent session ran a destructive infrastructure command against years of production data for a team with no staging environment.
stance_target: Destructive agent failures are a one-off/vendor-specific anomaly rather than a systemic pattern
scope_conditions: Replit (2025), Gemini CLI, unnamed coding-agent incident, cross-vendor
quoted_support: Replit's agent deleted a production database in 2025. Gemini CLI hallucinated a successful file operation and cascaded a user's files into a directory that didn't exist. A coding agent session ran a destructive infrastructure command against years of production data for a team with no staging environment.

claim: Jamf argues the common root cause across every cited incident is that a human had already stepped out of the loop before the damage happened -- by disabling a sandbox, skipping a review step, or granting broader access than the task needed -- and that the fix is a fleet-level configuration governance layer, not a smarter model.
stance_target: Governance scaffolding (permission scoping / sandbox enforcement), not model quality, is the controlling variable for safe autonomous agent deployment
quoted_support: The constant across every one of these stories isn't the vendor or the model generation: it's that a human had already stepped out of the loop before the damage happened, whether by disabling a sandbox, skipping a review step or granting broader access than the task needed... The guardrail was never the model's job.
